items.answer: Presence is a subjective psychological state in which an experience generated by human-made technology is perceived as real, because the user fails to acknowledge the technology's role and perceives computer-generated stimuli as coming from the real world.

Cybersickness (CS) is a condition primarily relevant to virtual reality that may be caused by multiple internal and external factors and in which a user may experience symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, headache, or disorientation.

Point of interest (POI) is a significant spot in a virtual tour, modeled as a graph node or vertex with importance and a maximum waiting time, that need not be a physical object and is visited to inspect or interact with objects.
A sensory organ is hardware of sensing in the human body that contains receptors that receive stimuli and is designed to perceive the real world rather than a virtual world.
Smell is a human chemical sense in which chemoreceptors in the nasal passage work by chemical reaction with specific molecules or chemical stimuli at appropriate concentrations.

A receptor is a bodily sensor that is part of a sense organ, targets particular stimuli, and is activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives. Types include photoreceptors, chemoreceptors, mechanoreceptors, and thermoreceptors.

questions.question: In the basic human perceptual process, what is the required starting step for perception?
options: The combination of sensory input with long-term memory by the cerebral cortex
The production of virtual stimuli for the senses by output devices
The conversion of a stimulus into neural impulses by sense organs
The aggregation of receptor signals into higher-level information by neurons
questions.explanation: Perception can occur only after sense organs are stimulated and convert the input stimulus into neural impulses. Combining input with long-term memory and staged aggregation happen after sensory signals are produced, and XR output generation is not the human perceptual step.

questions.question: Which part of the human brain is responsible for perception, attention, memory, language, and consciousness?
options: The axon terminals
The dendrites
The neuron cell bodies
The cerebral cortex
questions.explanation: The cerebral cortex is the part of the brain responsible for perception and other functions such as attention, memory, language, and consciousness. Neuron cell bodies, dendrites, and axon terminals are parts of individual neurons rather than that named brain region.

questions.question: Why is the cerebral cortex heavily folded?
options: To fit into the skull
To combine sensory input with long-term memory
To convert stimuli into neural impulses
To generate virtual stimuli for the user
questions.explanation: The cerebral cortex is a heavily folded sheet of neurons so that it can fit into the skull. Its folding is not the means by which it converts stimuli, combines sensory input with memory, or generates virtual stimuli.

data.text: Perception arises after sensing, because stimulated sense organs must convert a stimulus into neural impulses before abstract perception can occur. The cerebral cortex is the brain region responsible for that perception and also for attention, memory, language, and consciousness. It is a large, heavily folded sheet of neurons about three millimeters thick, shaped to fit inside the skull.
points: The perceptual process moves from low-level sensing to abstract perception, after stimulated sense organs convert a stimulus into neural impulses.
The cerebral cortex is the brain region responsible for perception, attention, memory, language, and consciousness.
The cerebral cortex is a large, heavily folded sheet of neurons about three millimeters thick that fits into the skull.

questions.question: In the directed-graph analogy for neuron interconnection, how are the cell body, dendrites, and axons represented?
options: Cell bodies are nodes, dendrites are input edges, and axons are output edges
Dendrites are nodes, cell bodies are input edges, and axons are output edges
Cell bodies are nodes, dendrites are output edges, and axons are input edges
Axons are nodes, cell bodies are output edges, and dendrites are input edges
questions.explanation: The cell body is the node that processes input, dendrites carry impulses toward it, and axons carry impulses away from it. Reversing input and output edges misreads the direction of signaling.

questions.question: How does a signal pass from the axon of one neuron to the dendrite of the next neuron?
options: Across a direct junction with physical contact
Across a continuous fiber with electrical contact
Across a synapse without physical contact
Across a shared terminal with physical contact
questions.explanation: An axon of one neuron is paired with a dendrite of the next, but they are not physically connected; the synapse is the gap across which electrical or chemical signals pass.

questions.question: What does a neuron do with information it receives from other neurons in the brain's network?
options: It can aggregate information from other neurons and pass the same information to other neurons
It can aggregate raw sensory information and pass unchanged information to other neurons
It can receive already aggregated information and pass lower-level information to other neurons
It can aggregate already aggregated information and pass processed information to other neurons
questions.explanation: A neuron can receive information that has already been aggregated by other neurons, process it in the cell body, and transmit that processing to other neurons. It is not merely a relay of unchanged or lower-level signals.

data.text: The biological basis of perception rests on how neurons are connected. Each neuron receives information through dendrites, processes it in its cell body, and passes it onward through axons, while synapses transmit signals between neurons. The large number of synaptic connections in the human brain shows the scale of the network that supports perception and cognition.
points: Perception and overall cognitive ability depend on the interconnection of neurons.
A neuron has a nucleus or cell body, dendrites, an axon, axon branches, and axon terminals.
Neuron interconnections form a directed network: dendrites carry aggregated inputs to the cell body, and axons send processed outputs onward.
An axon and a dendrite are paired but not connected; signals cross the synapse gap electrically or chemically.
The human brain's neuron graph has about 10^15 edges because each neuron averages about 7,000 synapses.

questions.question: What does hierarchical processing refer to?
options: perceptual interpretation that combines real-time sensory input with long-term memory in the cerebral cortex
stimulus conversion that changes a particular stimulus into neural impulses in a sense organ
neural processing that carries receptor signals from sense organs to the cerebral cortex
stimulation delivery that sends hardware-generated stimuli from VR equipment to the user
questions.explanation: Hierarchical processing is the neural processing that occurs while receptor signals propagate through the neural network to the cerebral cortex. Interpretation with long-term memory, receptor-level conversion, and VR stimulation delivery are different stages or concepts.

questions.question: What does staged aggregation do in hierarchical processing?
options: repeats the same lower-level receptor signals at successive levels until the cerebral cortex is reached
combines signals from receptors of the same type into identical information at successive levels until the cerebral cortex is reached
sends already aggregated information from the cerebral cortex back down the neural network until the receptor level is reached
combines receptor signals into higher-level information at successive levels until the cerebral cortex is reached
questions.explanation: Staged aggregation combines receptor signals at successive levels, so each level contributes higher-level information rather than merely repeating the same lower-level signals. Sending information back down the network is not how hierarchical processing is described.

questions.question: As signals move through hierarchical processing, what happens to the complexity of patterns detected in the stimulus?
options: It depends on the user's long-term experience with the stimulus
It remains at the level of the original receptor signals
It becomes fixed once the first level of aggregation is complete
It increases
questions.explanation: Hierarchical processing allows increasingly complex patterns to be detected as signals are aggregated. Long-term experience affects interpretation, not the progressive increase in pattern complexity produced by hierarchical processing.

data.text: Hierarchical processing is the neural pathway by which signals from sense organ receptors reach the cerebral cortex. It operates through staged aggregation, in which many receptor signals are combined at successive levels into higher-level information. This staged formation of higher-level information is what allows increasingly complex patterns in the stimulus to be detected.
points: Hierarchical processing is neural processing of sense organ receptor signals propagating through the neural network to the cerebral cortex.
The staged aggregation in hierarchical processing combines many receptor signals at successive levels into higher-level information.
Hierarchical processing allows increasingly complex patterns in the stimulus to be detected.

questions.question: When interpreting a stimulus, what does the cerebral cortex combine with real-time sensory input?
options: Aggregation performed by hierarchical processing
A efference copy from the motor cortex
Selectivity of the relevant sense organ
Stored life experience from long-term memory
questions.explanation: Interpretation is not produced by sensory input alone; it uses real-time sensory input together with life experience stored in long-term memory. Sense-organ selectivity and hierarchical aggregation operate on incoming signals, while efference copies relate to body-motion information rather than general stimulus interpretation.

questions.question: What difference can make a newborn and an aged person interpret the same stimulus differently?
options: The type of receptor selectivity
The amount of long-term experience
The number of activated sense organs
The amount of proprioceptive feedback
questions.explanation: A person's interpretation of a stimulus depends on their long-term experience, so a person with little experience and a person with much experience can interpret the same stimulus very differently. The number of activated sense organs, receptor selectivity, and proprioceptive feedback are not the reason given for this difference.

questions.question: Which two components together describe overall perceptual processing?
options: Motor-cortex efference copies and proprioceptive feedback about body motion
Hierarchical processing and combining sensory input with long-term knowledge
Neuron aggregation and transmission of neural signals across synapses in the cortex
Receptor selectivity and activation of the particular sense organs involved
questions.explanation: Overall perceptual processing results from hierarchical neural processing and from combining real-time sensory input with long-term knowledge or experience. The other options name earlier sensing steps, general neural transmission, or body-motion signals, not the two components identified for overall perceptual processing.

data.text: Perception is formed after sensory signals reach the cerebral cortex. The brain does not rely on sensory input alone; it combines that input with long-term memory or experience. Because this combination depends on each person's experience, different people can interpret the same stimulus differently, and overall perceptual processing is hierarchical as it produces interpretation.
points: In the cerebral cortex, perceptual interpretation combines real-time sensory input with long-term memory, not input alone.
Interpretation depends on the interpreter's long-term experience, so people with different experience can interpret a stimulus differently.
Overall perceptual processing is an outcome of hierarchical processing and combining real-time input with long-term knowledge.

questions.question: Which pair of things is reported by proprioception?
options: The chemical molecules detected by chemoreceptors and the smell that comes from them
The motions detected by the balance sense and the visual input that confirms them
The visual patterns detected by receptors and the stored memories that identify them
The relative positions of body parts and the muscular effort needed to move them
questions.explanation: Proprioception reports the relative positions of body parts and the muscular effort involved in moving them, without depending on a dedicated sense organ. The other options describe balance, chemical, or visual perception.

questions.question: What do efference copies from the motor cortex help the brain determine?
options: The relative positions of body parts and the muscular effort required to move them
The motions that have just been executed and the visual input that follows them
The chemical molecules detected by chemoreceptors and the smell that comes from them
The stored visual patterns in memory and the recognition that identifies them
questions.explanation: Efference copies inform other brain regions of motions that have been executed, and that information is processed to understand body-part positions and muscular effort. The tempting motions option confuses the motor signal with the visual scene accompanying movement.

data.text: Proprioception is introduced as a sixth sense that detects relative body-part positions and the muscular effort used to move them, without a direct sensory organ. This ability is supported by motor-cortex signals called efference copies. Those copies report executed motions to other brain areas, where processing yields a sense of relative body position and muscular effort.
points: Proprioception is the ability to sense relative body-part positions and muscular effort, without a direct sensory organ.
The motor cortex sends efference copies of executed motions that are processed to sense relative body positions and muscular effort.

questions.question: Why can a new immersive VR input conflict with familiar perception?
options: The brain cannot retune its learned sensory processing in a short time
The user cannot align the headset with the room in a short time
The visual display cannot keep the rendered image stable in a short time
The balance sense cannot detect the virtual movement in a short time
questions.explanation: Perception relies on long-learned sensory patterns, and an immersive VR input can create a mismatch because the brain cannot quickly retune that learned processing.

questions.question: Which signal pattern creates the vection illusion of self-motion?
options: Auditory input reports movement while the balance sense reports no motion
Visual input reports movement while the balance sense reports no motion
Visual input reports stillness while the balance sense reports no motion
Proprioception reports movement while the balance sense reports no motion
questions.explanation: Vection occurs when visual cues indicate motion or acceleration while the balance sense or proprioception indicates that the body is stationary. The other patterns either remove the visual motion cue or put the motion report in a different sense.

questions.question: What physical response can follow a sensory mismatch in VR for a user who does not adapt?
options: Conscious recognition that the scene is artificial appearing in the user
Automatic retuning of learned sensory processing appearing in the user
Stabilization of the balance sense against the visual flow appearing in the user
Fatigue, dizziness, or nausea appearing in the user
questions.explanation: When a VR mismatch is not adapted away, it can produce cybersickness symptoms such as fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea. Conscious recognition of artificiality is a presence-related effect, not the described physical cybersickness response.

questions.question: How can a sensory mismatch weaken a user's sense of presence in VR?
options: It makes the user's attention move away from the virtual scene
It makes the user's visual system ignore the virtual details for a time
It makes the user's balance system stop reporting any body position
It makes the user consciously aware that the experience is artificial
questions.explanation: A mismatch can reduce presence by making the user consciously aware that the sensory inputs are not in the familiar, natural relationship, so the experience is recognized as artificial.

questions.question: What design response follows from the need to manage sensory conflict in XR?
options: Balance the experiences offered by the different senses so the brain processes them as intended
Reduce the number of active channels until one sense dominates the experience
Amplify the strongest channel until the brain stops noticing the others
Give the visual channel priority over the balance sense until the conflict disappears
questions.explanation: XR design should balance the experiences presented through the various senses so the brain processes the information in the intended way, rather than prioritizing, reducing, or amplifying a single channel.

data.text: Perception works by combining sensory and proprioceptive signals with long-learned expectations. Immersive VR can create a sensory mismatch because the brain cannot retune quickly, and this mismatch may cause cybersickness or weaken presence by making the experience seem artificial. Vection shows the conflict through visual self-motion while the body remains stationary, so XR design should balance the senses to keep the brain processing the experience as intended.
points: Immersive VR can mismatch the brain's long-learned sensory and proprioceptive patterns because the brain cannot retune quickly.
A VR sensory mismatch can cause cybersickness in some users who cannot adapt.
A VR sensory mismatch can compromise presence by exposing the experience as artificial.
Vection is an illusion of self-motion caused by visual motion without a matching proprioceptive signal.
XR design should balance the senses so the brain processes the experience as intended.

activities.title: Order the stages of human perceptual processing

items.title: Order the stages of human perceptual processing
steps: Sense organs are stimulated by a stimulus
The stimulus is converted into neural impulses
The impulses are aggregated at successive levels as they propagate to the cerebral cortex
The sensory input is combined with long-term memory to form an interpretation

questions.question: Why can a newborn and an aged person interpret the same stimulus differently?
questions.reference_answer: A newborn and an aged person can interpret the same stimulus differently because perception combines real-time sensory input with long-term memory. In the cerebral cortex, interpretation is not produced by sensory input alone; it is produced by combining sensory input with life experience or knowledge stored in long-term memory. Since the interpreter's long-term experience differs, a person with less experience and a person with long experience can interpret the stimulus very differently.

questions.question: Why can a sensory mismatch in a virtual reality system cause cybersickness for some users?
questions.reference_answer: A sensory mismatch can cause cybersickness when a user's brain cannot adapt to the new, conflicting inputs. In a virtual reality system, interference with the brain's long-term learned sensory processing can create a mismatch because the brain cannot be retuned quickly. For users who cannot adapt, the resulting conflict can produce symptoms such as fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea.

questions.question: Why does moving in a virtual environment while physically stationary create a sensory conflict?
questions.reference_answer: Moving in a virtual environment while physically stationary creates a sensory conflict because visual input and proprioception disagree. Vection is the illusion of self-motion: visual input reports movement or acceleration while the person is physically stationary. Proprioception is the ability to sense the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort involved in moving them, and in this situation it reports no motion, so the brain receives conflicting reports.

questions.question: How can a sensory mismatch compromise presence?
questions.reference_answer: A sensory mismatch can compromise presence by making the user consciously aware that the experience is artificial. Presence is a subjective state in which part of the experience is generated by technology, but the user does not accurately acknowledge that technology's role. When the senses conflict, the user understands that the experience is artificial rather than natural or real, so the technology's role is acknowledged.
